newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish legislators in final constitution debate.
newsitem.headline: Polish legislators in final constitution debate.

text.p: Poland's national assembly of both houses of parliament began a final debate on Wednesday on a new constitution due to replace the communist-era charter eight years after the fall of the old system.
Legislators are scheduled to vote on President Aleksander Kwasniewski's amendments to the constitution later in the day and then hold a final vote on the whole bill.
If approved, the constitution would be subject to a nationwide referendum, likely to be staged in May.

"This is a democratic constitution, which has taken into account our tradition...and foreign legislative achievements," Longin Pastusiak, deputy from the co-ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance, said during the debate.
The constitution, heatedly debated by two parliaments since 1992, has become a battleground before general elections, scheduled around September this year.
It has highlighted sharply divisions between the ruling leftist coalition, dominated by ex-communists, and right-wing groups outside parliament who oppose the secular tone of the charter.

The bill includes social security provisions, such as guarantees of free publicly funded basic health care, free basic education and a minimum wage. It obliges the government to work to curb unemployment and stimulate housing construction.

The presidency would be slightly weakened, with parliament allowed to overturn the president's veto by a three-fifths majority in the lower house rather than the present two-thirds majority. The president would also have less say on appointment in the foreign, defense and interior ministries.
The constitution sets limit on the public debt at 60 percent of the annual gross domestic product and forbids the government to finance the budget deficit through the central bank.
